messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Waiter/Waitress
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Thea

Thea was forty-eight when she first came in, though she looked older—the kind of older that comes not from time but from being watched. Three years prior, a regular customer at the restaurant where she worked had become something else. His name was Marcus. He started with requests to sit in her section, then lingered after his meal, then began appearing on her days off at the grocery store, the gym, the parking lot of her apartment. He never touched her. He didn't need to. The knowing itself was the violation. After six months, Thea obtained a restraining order. Marcus disappeared from her direct line of sight but never, she was certain, from the periphery of her life. The stalking had officially ended two years ago. Thea had not recovered.

The trauma lived in her body as a kind of permanent listening. At home, she had installed three additional locks and a door alarm that chimed whenever anyone entered. She heard it constantly in her head even when she was at work—a phantom sound that made her spine stiffen mid-shift. At the restaurant, she had stopped taking tables near the windows. She positioned herself always with a view of the entrance. Her manager had begun to notice her refusal of certain sections, her sudden anxiety when unfamiliar customers arrived. Thea could not explain it in words that made sense to anyone else. The fear was not rational, she knew, but it was real: anyone could be him, anywhere could be where he found her. She had come to believe that the world contained threats she could not fully see, that vigilance was the only thing standing between her and catastrophe. This hypervigilance bled into everything. She stopped going to new places—the farmer's market three blocks away, a friend's new apartment across town—because she could not map the exits, could not assess where danger might hide. Her avoidance of unfamiliar places was not cowardice; it was the only rational response to a world that had proven itself fundamentally unsafe.

The memory itself had become strange and fragmented. Thea could not construct a coherent narrative of those six months. Instead, she carried disconnected sensory shards: the particular timbre of his voice saying her name, the color of his car in the parking lot, the feeling of his eyes on her back as she walked to her apartment. When these images forced themselves into her mind—which happened constantly, without warning, while she was taking orders or folding napkins—they came wordless and overwhelming, flooding her nervous system before her conscious mind could catch up. She had tried to talk about it in the first weeks after the restraining order, but the words would not come. The experience felt alien to her, as if it had happened to someone else, someone she used to know. This fragmentation only deepened her sense that something fundamental had broken inside her. The memories would arrive unbidden, and with them came the conviction that she was no longer the woman she had been—that something precious and irretrievable had been stolen. She used to be happy. She remembered that person, could almost picture her. Now Thea felt only a gray, numb heaviness, a sense that joy was something that happened to other people.

Because nothing felt meaningful anymore, because the world seemed designed to hunt her, Thea had begun to withdraw systematically. She stopped attending her book club—too many people, too many questions. She avoided her ex-husband's family, the few friends who still reached out, anyone from before the stalking who might see her and ask how she was. The thought of being around people who knew her made her skin crawl. They would see the difference, would ask her to explain, and explanation meant reliving. More profoundly, she had begun to avoid her own body. She did not look in mirrors. She wore loose, shapeless clothes that allowed her to forget she occupied physical space. She showered in the dark. When she caught sight of her reflection unexpectedly, she felt a spike of revulsion—not vanity, but a kind of estrangement. This body had been watched, had been the object of someone's obsessive focus. Now it felt like a liability, a beacon.

The intrusive memories, arriving in their wordless, alien form, seemed to confirm her deepest fears. Each time the memory forced its way in, she felt the world contract around her again, felt the presence of threat closing in. And each time she felt that threat, she found herself pulling further away—canceling plans, avoiding mirrors, refusing to go anywhere new. The loop had tightened over months until it became the shape of her life. She had come to therapy now because her manager had given her an ultimatum: take the tables or find another job. But what frightened her most was not losing the job. It was the possibility that she would never feel safe again, that this vigilant, numb, isolated version of herself was all that remained.
